newsitem.title: USA: Brief warm-up then plunge in U.S. temps forecast.
newsitem.headline: Brief warm-up then plunge in U.S. temps forecast.

text.p: Weather forecasters said Tuesday that temperatures in the "heating oil belt" in the northeastern United States will warm up over the next couple of days but then plunge for at least a week.
Texas also is expected to have a brief warm period before sinking back to new record-low temperatures.
"Today's maps look considerably colder for next week," said Charles Notis, a meteorologist at Freese-Notis in Des Moines, Iowa.

"If you go by today's maps, roughly the entire eastern half of the country will be much below normal. It could be the longest stretch of sustained cold for the northeast that we've had this year," Notis added.
"The northeast will see continued cold except for a small mild period," according to widely-watched forecasters at brokerage Smith Barney.
The northeastern part is the largest market for heating oil in the United States.

The National Weather Service, in its six-to-10 day forecast starting on January 19, sees temperatures in both the northeast and in Texas at levels "much below normal," which means at least six degrees below the seasonal average.

Weather Services Corp also forecasts for Texas "a brief warm-up Wednesday and Thursday before arctic air returns later this week," with "much below normal temperatures," though just "below normal" temperatures for the northeast.

"The difference between yesterday and today is that the jet stream which was becoming more east to west (is now showing), on both main forecast models, a flow from north central Siberia circumventing the Arctic Circle and straight south toward the U.S.," said Notis.

For New York, the outlook is for a warm up to the mid-40s Fahrenheit in the next two days before a plunge. In Texas, the Houston area is expected to warm up to the 50s Fahrenheit over the next couple of days but after that temperatures are expected to set new record-lows, breaking those set in the last couple of days, said Notis.
((-- Tony McAuley, New York Energy Desk, + 1 212 859 1623))
